elements.element: Audits may occur no more than once in any 12-month period.
elements.evidence: Section 22.1 permits audits “no more than once in any 12 months.”

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 30 days' notice of an audit.
Audit notice must be in writing.
Audits must be conducted during business hours.
elements.evidence: The added operative sentence states that the audit “shall be conducted during business hours.”

elements.element: Audits must be conducted by an independent auditor.
elements.evidence: The added operative sentence requires the audit to be conducted “by an independent auditor.”

elements.element: The independent auditor must be bound by confidentiality.
elements.evidence: The added operative sentence requires an independent auditor “bound by confidentiality.”

elements.element: Vendor must bear audit costs unless the audit establishes an underpayment exceeding 5% for the audited period.
elements.evidence: Section 22.2 and the added sentence both impose Vendor cost responsibility unless underpayment exceeds 5% for the audited period.

elements.element: Vendor and its auditor must have no direct access to Customer systems.
elements.evidence: Section 22.2 expressly provides that “Vendor and its auditor may not access Customer systems directly”; section 22.1 also removes remote system access.

elements.element: Audits may occur no more than once per year.
elements.evidence: The stricter limit of no more than once in any 12 months satisfies the annual-frequency requirement.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 15 days' notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: The clause requires 30 days' written notice, which exceeds the 15-day fallback minimum.

elements.element: Vendor must bear audit costs unless the audit establishes an underpayment exceeding 10%.
elements.evidence: The clause shifts reasonable audit costs to Customer when underpayment exceeds 5%, including underpayments above 5% but not exceeding 10%; therefore, the required 10% exception threshold is absent.

result.reason: All preferred requirements are operative. The fallback cost threshold is not met because the clause uses 5% rather than 10%. The redline is not minimal because it redundantly restates the cost rule and adds an unrequested “off-site where possible” condition. Those additions do not contradict the audit provisions or impair unrelated commercial terms, but the duplication and undefined off-site qualification reduce drafting quality.
